strengths: Provides a novel interpretation of the fully first-order F2SA method as using forward finite differences to approximate the hyper-gradient, which naturally motivates a family of higher-order methods.

Proposes F2SA-p, a general algorithm using pth-order finite differences, and proves an improved SFO complexity of O(p ε^{-4-2/p}) for pth-order smooth bilevel problems, generalizing prior O(ε^{-6}) results.
Establishes a matching Ω(ε^{-4}) lower bound via a simple separable construction, showing near-optimality in the highly smooth regime p = Ω(log ε^{-1}/loglog ε^{-1}).
The technical analysis is nontrivial, leveraging the high-dimensional Faà di Bruno formula and an induction argument to bound high-order derivatives of the perturbed lower-level solution map.
The proposed F2SA-2 is shown to outperform several baselines on a standard learn-to-regularize bilevel benchmark, supporting the practical potential of the method.
weaknesses: The main acceleration relies on a strong additional high-order smoothness assumption in the lower-level variable y (Assumption 2.5), which may be difficult to verify or satisfy in many practical bilevel problems.

The lower bound Ω(ε^{-4}) is not tight for small p (especially p=1), so the paper leaves a significant gap in the standard first-order smooth setting; the separable construction may also not capture true bilevel hardness.

The empirical evaluation is limited to a single dataset and lacks important details such as SFO counts, wall-clock time, code, and hyperparameter search specifics; only p=2 is shown to be practically beneficial, while larger p is not demonstrated.

The algorithm presentation has some technical inconsistencies: Algorithm 1 loops over j=0 for even p even though the central difference coefficient is zero, wasting an extra lower-level solve, and the finite difference lemma for odd p contains typographical errors in the summation and coefficient definitions.
The abstract states the improved bound as O(p ε^{4-p/2}), which is likely a typo for O(p ε^{-4-2/p}); this could confuse readers.
The complexity bound has a high condition-number dependence (κ^{9+2/p}), and the parameter choices depend on unknown constants and the target accuracy ε, which may limit practical applicability.

strengths: Proposes a novel connection between F2SA and finite-difference approximation of the hyper-gradient, leading to a general p-th-order method F2SA-p.
Provides a theoretical upper bound O(p ε^{-4-2/p}) for p-th-order smooth bilevel problems, improving the ε^{-6} rate for sufficiently smooth instances.

Extends an Ω(ε^{-4}) lower bound to stochastic bilevel optimization via a separable construction, showing that the ε^{-4} barrier persists even under high-order smoothness in the lower-level variable.
Includes numerical experiments on the standard learn-to-regularize benchmark, showing that F2SA-2 can outperform F2SA and HVP-based methods in practice.
weaknesses: The abstract reports an incorrect complexity, O(p ε^{4-p/2}), which is inconsistent with the main theorem's O(p ε^{-4-2/p}). This is a serious presentation error.

Algorithm 1 for even p loops over j = -p/2, ..., p/2, including j = 0, even though the central-difference coefficient satisfies α_0 = 0. Thus it solves p+1 lower-level problems, not p as claimed, contradicting the pT(S+K) complexity and the statement that F2SA-2 needs only two lower-level solves.

The theoretical improvement relies on a strong and unusual high-order smoothness assumption only in y. For practical values, the gain is modest: p=1 gives no rate improvement, and p=2 improves ε^{-6} to ε^{-5} only under additional second-order smoothness.

The strong convexity of the perturbed lower-level problems g_{jν} for j up to p/2 is not adequately justified. The proof states ν = O(1/κ), but strong convexity requires |j|ν = O(1/κ); this may impose additional constraints on p, ν, or κ that are not addressed.

The lower bound is obtained from a fully separable instance where the lower-level problem is trivial and the bilevel problem reduces to single-level optimization. It is valid but weak: it does not capture bilevel-specific hardness and does not justify the tightness of the upper bound for moderate p.

The experiments are limited to a single benchmark, do not compare SFO-call complexity or wall-clock time, and lack details on random seeds, error bars, and implementation. The theoretical complexity improvement is not convincingly validated empirically.

The near-optimality claim in the highly smooth regime requires p = Ω(log ε^{-1}/log log ε^{-1}), i.e., the order of smoothness must grow as ε decreases. This is an unrealistic regime and limits the practical significance of the result.

There are several technical/writing inconsistencies, e.g., Lemma 3.1's odd-p sum is written over j = -p/2,...,p/2 while the coefficients are defined for j = 0,...,p, and Algorithm 1 does not match the described p-point finite-difference scheme.

strengths: Novel and insightful reinterpretation of F2SA as a forward finite-difference approximation of the hyper-gradient, leading to a natural generalization F2SA-p using higher-order finite differences.

Provides improved SFO complexity bounds for p-th order smooth bilevel problems, with near-optimality in the highly smooth regime p = Ω(log ε^{-1}/log log ε^{-1}), matching the Ω(ε^{-4}) lower bound up to logarithmic factors.
Rigorous theoretical analysis, including a high-dimensional Faà di Bruno formula application, careful condition-number dependencies, and detailed proofs in the appendix.
The lower-bound construction via a separable bilevel instance is simple and valid under the stated assumptions, filling a gap in prior lower bounds for stochastic bilevel optimization.
Experiments on the standard learn-to-regularize benchmark show that F2SA-2 outperforms several baselines, including HVP-based methods, supporting the practical potential of the proposed method.
Paper is well-organized, clearly positions itself relative to prior work, and discusses open problems transparently.
weaknesses: The main acceleration relies on strong high-order smoothness assumptions in the lower-level variable y; for typical first-order smooth problems, the improvement is only a constant-factor condition-number improvement, leaving a significant gap to the lower bound for small p.

Practical benefits are limited: higher p requires solving more lower-level problems per iteration, and experiments find p=2 to be the best choice; the near-optimal regime requires p to grow with 1/ε, which is unrealistic in practice.

The Ω(ε^{-4}) lower bound is derived from a fully separable construction where the bilevel problem reduces exactly to single-level optimization; while valid, it is not surprising and may not capture inherent bilevel hardness.

Experimental evaluation is preliminary: only one small-scale dataset (20 Newsgroup) and one task are used, with no comparisons in terms of SFO calls or wall-clock time, making it difficult to verify the practical complexity claims.
The abstract contains an apparent typo in the complexity exponent (O(p ε^{4-p/2})), which is inconsistent with the correct bound O(p ε^{-4-2/p}) in the theorem; this should be fixed.

The condition-number dependence is high (κ^{9+2/p}), and the algorithm uses a normalized gradient step whose necessity is not fully resolved; the paper remarks that standard gradient steps likely work but does not prove it.

strengths: Novel interpretation of F2SA as forward difference for hyper-gradient approximation, leading to a general F2SA-p algorithm using pth-order finite differences.

Theoretical improvement: for pth-order smooth bilevel problems, achieves O(p ε^{-4-2/p}) SFO complexity, recovering near-optimal O(ε^{-4}) when p is large; F2SA-2 improves over F2SA without extra per-iteration cost.
Provides an Ω(ε^{-4}) lower bound for stochastic bilevel optimization under high-order smoothness of the lower-level variable, showing near-optimality of F2SA-p in the highly smooth regime.
Generalizes prior finite-difference connections in meta-learning to general bilevel optimization and arbitrary order p, and tightens existing bounds for p=2.
Experiments on logistic regression and MLP tasks demonstrate empirical benefits of F2SA-p over F2SA and HVP-based baselines.
weaknesses: Experiments compare performance per outer iteration rather than per SFO call or runtime; for p>2, F2SA-p solves p lower-level problems per outer iteration, so the practical cost is not fairly reflected in the plots.

The strong convexity of the perturbed lower-level problems g_{jν}=g+jν f requires |j|ν to be sufficiently small for all j up to p/2; the paper's parameter setting and proof do not explicitly verify this condition for all j, which could be a technical gap.
The high-order smoothness assumption (Assumption 2.5) is strong and only imposed on the lower-level variable y, potentially limiting applicability beyond specially smooth problems.
The upper bound has a large condition number dependence κ^{9+2/p}, which is worse than several known lower bounds (e.g., κ^4 or κ^{5/2}), so the result is not near-optimal in terms of κ.

The lower bound is obtained by a straightforward reduction to single-level optimization using a separable instance with deterministic lower-level problem, so it may not fully capture bilevel-specific hardness.
The improvement for p=1 (from κ^{12}ε^{-6} to κ^{11}ε^{-6}) is minor; the main gains require p≥2 and stronger smoothness assumptions.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: complexity of fully first-order stochastic bilevel optimization, and gives a new perspective by interpreting F2SA as forward finite-difference approximation.

Proposes F2SA-p, a general class of algorithms based on higher-order finite differences, with a theoretical upper bound that improves the prior O(ε^{-6}) to O(p ε^{-4-2/p}) under p-th-order smoothness in the lower-level variable.
Provides a non-trivial Faà di Bruno-based analysis for high-order smoothness in ν and derives improved condition-number dependence for p=1 and p=2.
Includes a lower-bound construction showing Ω(ε^{-4}) for stochastic bilevel problems via a reduction to single-level optimization, which is a valid, if simple, complement to the upper bounds.
Contains numerical experiments on learn-to-regularize logistic regression and an MLP, demonstrating the proposed methods can be competitive in practice.
weaknesses: The central acceleration relies on a strong high-order smoothness assumption only in the lower-level variable, and the condition number κ hides high-order smoothness constants L_p; for large p the problem class can be very restrictive, and the claimed improvement may not hold for realistic bilevel problems.

The technical analysis has potentially serious gaps: Lemma 3.1 states O(Cν^p) without controlling the dependence of the constant on p, while standard finite-difference coefficients have error constants that grow exponentially with p; similarly, the Faà di Bruno expansion in Lemma 3.2 involves a number of partitions (Bell number) that grows super-exponentially, and the paper does not account for these p-dependent factors. These omitted constants could invalidate the claimed near-optimal Õ(ε^{-4}) rate for p = Ω(log(1/ε)/loglog(1/ε)).

Novelty is incremental: the finite-difference interpretation of F2SA is natural, and the lower bound is essentially a trivial separable reduction to the single-level lower bound of Arjevani et al. (2023). The main contribution is an application of standard higher-order finite differences rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The experimental evaluation is weak and potentially misleading: the methods are compared per outer iteration rather than per stochastic first-order oracle call or wall-clock time, despite F2SA-p for p>2 solving p lower-level subproblems per outer iteration. This makes the reported comparisons unfair and does not substantiate the claimed computational speedups.

The practical significance of the improved complexity is unclear: for p=1 the gain is only a κ factor over prior work, and for p>1 the algorithm requires p lower-level SGD subroutines per outer step, increasing per-iteration cost and tuning overhead. The paper does not discuss this trade-off or provide SFO-based empirical validation.

The lower bound does not close the gap for p=1 or address condition-number dependency; the paper explicitly leaves these open, so the main claims of near-optimality are limited to an asymptotic regime with strong smoothness and constant condition number.

Clarity and presentation issues: inconsistent notation (F2SA vs F^{2}SA), typos, an erroneous table entry labeling F2SA-p as “1st-order”, and several hyperparameter settings in Theorem 3.1 appear to ignore constant factors needed for the NSGD convergence lemma to strictly yield an ε-stationary point.

The algorithm modifies F2SA to use normalized gradient descent, but the claimed equivalence to standard gradient steps is not proved; the effect of this normalization on the finite-difference bias and on practical performance is not analyzed.

strengths: Provides a novel and insightful interpretation of F2SA as forward finite-difference approximation of the hyper-gradient, which naturally motivates a general class of F2SA-p methods.

Establishes rigorous theoretical improvements: for pth-order smooth problems, the upper bound improves to O(p epsilon^{-4-2/p}) (up to condition-number factors), and for large p it matches the lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

Proves an Omega(epsilon^{-4}) lower bound for stochastic bilevel optimization via a valid separable construction, complementing the upper bounds and showing near-optimality in the highly smooth regime.
The technical lemmas, especially the finite-difference coefficient construction and the high-order smoothness analysis via Faa di Bruno, are carefully derived and extend prior results to general p.
Experiments on learn-to-regularize illustrate the practical potential of F2SA-2 and larger p, showing improved test loss/accuracy over F2SA and HVP-based baselines.
The paper is clearly written, well motivated, and positions the contribution appropriately within the bilevel optimization literature.
weaknesses: The condition-number dependence of the upper bound remains high (e.g., kappa^{9+2/p}), and the gap to lower bounds is large; the paper acknowledges this but does not resolve it.

The experimental evaluation is limited to two small-scale settings and compares only outer-loop iterations, not wall-clock time or SFO calls; since F2SA-p solves p lower-level problems per outer iteration, the reported iteration-based comparisons may overstate practical efficiency for larger p.

The lower bound is obtained from a separable construction where the lower-level problem is trivial (quadratic, independent of x), so it may not capture bilevel-specific hardness and does not provide condition-number-dependent lower bounds.
For the common first-order smooth case p=1, the improvement is only a factor of kappa, and for moderate p the gains over F2SA may be incremental in practice.

Algorithm 1 for even p in the main text includes j=0 in the parallel lower-level solves, even though the corresponding finite-difference coefficient is zero; this is a minor inconsistency with the claim that p points suffice for even p.
The code link is mentioned but not actually provided in the manuscript, and there is no detailed discussion of hyperparameter sensitivity or statistical variability in the experiments.
